title: Licences for AI Voices and Music

slide.title: Free to Make, Not Use
slide.body: A simple document with lines of small print, a teal magnifying glass over it, and a music note and sound wave icon on the page. Small tag: AI Voice, Audio and Music · Lesson 8.

production_notes: Licences are taught as principles only. The voiceover names no tool's terms and states no legal conclusion; this course gives no legal advice.

[VERIFY] [VERSION] content.md says free tiers often allow personal use only or add conditions for commercial use, while paid plans may allow more. The voiceover does not state this as fact: it says only that plans can have different terms and that learners must read the terms for the plan they used. Check against current official terms before adding any claim.

[VERIFY] [VERSION] content.md says some platforms ask for labels on realistic AI content and some detect music they believe is copyrighted. The voiceover says only that platforms have their own rules. Check current platform policies before adding detail.

[VERIFY] [REGION] Whether music or audio made mostly by AI can be protected by copyright is unsettled and differs by country (content.md and curriculum flag). The voiceover presents this only as an open question and tells learners to check official guidance in their country.
[VERSION] Attribution wording and output ownership vary by tool. The credit line on scene 5 uses the placeholder '[tool name]' on the slide only.

Aroha's example terms are hypothetical. Do not show any real tool's logo, name or terms page on the Aroha slides. Aroha and the Wellington tourism client are fictional. Pronunciation: Aroha = ah-ROH-ha.

Hook.voiceover: You made a voiceover and a music bed with free tools. Can you use them in a video that earns money? Can a client use them in an advert? The answers are not in the audio file. They are in the licence.
Hook.on_screen_text: The answer is in the licence

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you made a music bed. Today, we check what you are allowed to do with it. A licence is the set of permissions that tells you what you may do with something you did not fully create or own. For AI voices and music, it usually comes from the tool's terms of service.

slide.title: Licences for AI Voices and Music
slide.body: AI Voice, Audio and Music · Lesson 8 of 10

Explain.voiceover: A licence answers four main questions. The first is personal or commercial use. Personal use means projects that do not earn money, like a class assignment. Commercial use means anything connected to earning money, like a sponsored podcast, an advert or client work.

slide.title: 1. Personal or commercial?
slide.body: Left: Personal use: class assignment, family video. Right: Commercial use: monetised video, sponsored podcast, advert, client work.

Explain.voiceover: Free and paid plans can have different terms. So do not assume. Read the terms for the plan you actually used.
Explain.on_screen_text: Read the terms for your plan

Explain.voiceover: The second question is attribution. Some licences require you to credit the tool, for example in your show notes. If a credit is required, it is part of the licence, not a polite extra. The third question is platform rules. Video and podcast platforms have their own rules, and your content must follow them too.

slide.title: 2. Attribution · 3. Platform rules
slide.body: Attribution: e.g. 'Music made with [tool name]' in show notes: required, not optional · Platform rules: your content must follow the tool's licence AND the platform's rules

Explain.voiceover: The fourth question is who owns the output. Some tools say you own what you create. Others keep some rights, or give you a licence to use it. There is also a wider legal question about whether music made mostly by AI can be protected at all. This course gives no legal advice, so check current official guidance in your country.

slide.title: 4. Who owns the output?
slide.body: Some tools: you own it · Others: they keep some rights or give you a licence · Open question: protection for mostly-AI music depends on the country. Check official guidance.

Explain.voiceover: Here is a way to picture it. A licence is like the rules for a rented flat. The contract says whether you can run a business from it, or rent it to someone else. Keeping a signed copy means you can prove what was agreed.
Explain.on_screen_text: Keep a copy of the contract

Demonstrate.voiceover: That signed copy is your rights log. It is a simple table with one row for each asset. It records the tool and plan, a short summary of the licence, whether you need a credit, any consent for a real person's voice, the date you checked, and a link or screenshot.

slide.title: A rights log
slide.body: Table header row: Asset · Type · Tool and plan · Licence terms (short) · Attribution needed? · Consent needed/obtained? · Date checked · Link or screenshot. One empty row below.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see it in use. Aroha is a video creator in Wellington, in New Zealand. She has just signed her first paid project, for a local tourism business. Her video uses a text-to-speech voiceover and an AI music bed, both made on free plans. So she checks each asset.
Demonstrate.stock_query: video creator editing travel footage laptop

Demonstrate.voiceover: In her example, the voice tool's free plan does not allow commercial use, so she records her own voice instead. The music tool's free plan allows online videos, but requires a credit, so she adds a credit line. Then she checks the platform's current rules on AI labels, and adds the label that applies.

slide.title: Aroha checks each asset
slide.body: Voiceover: free plan, no commercial use (red cross) → records her own voice. Music bed: online videos allowed, credit required (amber) → adds credit line. Platform: AI label rules → adds label. Footer: example terms only.

Demonstrate.voiceover: She adds a row for each asset to her rights log, with the date and a screenshot of the terms. She also tells the client that the music is AI-generated. Remember, these terms are only examples. Real tools have different terms, so always read your own.

slide.title: Aroha's rights log
slide.body: Three filled rows: Voiceover (own recording, consent: self) · Music bed (AI tool, free plan, credit required, credit added) · Platform label (added). Each with a date and a screenshot icon.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to think that free to use means free for any use. It usually means free to create. What you may do with the result is in the licence. And check again before each new commercial project, because terms change.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Free to make is not free to use

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a licence tells you if you can use an asset commercially, if you must credit the tool, and what the tool says about ownership. Second, plans can have different terms, and platforms have their own rules. Third, keep a rights log for every voice and music asset, with the tool, plan, terms, consent and date.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Licence: commercial use · attribution · ownership. 2. Plans differ; platforms have their own rules. 3. Rights log: tool, plan, terms, consent, date for every asset.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will start a rights log for your project, with each voice and music asset, the tool, the plan, the licence terms and the date you checked. It takes about twenty-five minutes. You will submit this log with your capstone. In the next lesson, Mixing Voice and Music, we put it all together.
